questions.prompt: What do we call a cloud of tiny water droplets at ground level?
questions.hint: Its defining feature is where it forms.
questions.explanation: Fog is a cloud at or near the ground, often formed when moist air cools to saturation.

questions.prompt: Which cloud type is most closely associated with thunderstorms?
questions.hint: Look for the cloud with great vertical development.
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are deep convective clouds that produce thunderstorms.

questions.prompt: The pressure-gradient force initially pushes air in which direction?

choices.text: From lower pressure toward higher pressure
From higher pressure toward lower pressure

questions.hint: Other forces can turn the wind after it starts moving.
questions.explanation: A difference in pressure exerts a force from high toward low pressure. Rotation and friction modify the resulting wind.

questions.prompt: Air cooled at constant pressure without changing its water-vapor content reaches saturation at what temperature?
questions.hint: This threshold depends on the moisture already present.
questions.explanation: The dew point is the temperature to which air must cool to become saturated at constant pressure and water-vapor content.

questions.prompt: Broad layered clouds and steady precipitation ahead of an advancing front are classically associated with which type?
questions.hint: The advancing air rises gently over a cooler air mass.
questions.explanation: At a warm front, warm air gradually overruns cooler air, often producing widespread layered cloud and precipitation.

questions.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air toward which side of its motion?
questions.hint: This is a consequence of observing motion on a rotating planet.
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere the apparent horizontal deflection is to the right of the direction of travel.

questions.prompt: How does temperature change with height inside a temperature inversion?

choices.text: It falls at exactly 10 degrees Celsius per kilometer
It falls faster than in the air below

questions.hint: The name refers to a reversal of the usual lower-atmosphere pattern.
questions.explanation: In an inversion, warmer air lies above cooler air. This often suppresses vertical mixing.

questions.prompt: When water vapor condenses inside a rising cloud, what happens to latent heat?

choices.text: It is released to the surrounding air
It is absorbed from the surrounding air
It is converted entirely into wind momentum
It disappears without an energy transfer

questions.hint: Compare condensation with the energy needed for evaporation.
questions.explanation: Condensation releases latent heat, partly offsetting the cooling of a rising air parcel.

questions.prompt: An unsaturated parcel rises without exchanging heat and stays unsaturated. Roughly how much does it cool per kilometer?
questions.hint: Do not confuse a parcel's rate with an average observed atmospheric profile.
questions.explanation: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is about 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometer, commonly rounded to 10.

questions.prompt: Which contrast chiefly defines a dryline?

choices.text: A boundary between rain and snow at the ground
A boundary between surface wind and calm air aloft
A sharp change in atmospheric moisture
A sharp change in pressure without a moisture contrast

questions.hint: Temperature may also differ, but it is not the defining variable.
questions.explanation: A dryline separates relatively dry and moist air masses and can be marked by a sharp dew-point gradient.

questions.prompt: Why does a ventilated wet-bulb thermometer usually read below the dry-bulb temperature in unsaturated air?

choices.text: Condensation supplies energy to the wet bulb
Water increases the local air pressure
The wet covering blocks all infrared radiation
Evaporation takes energy from the wet bulb

questions.hint: Compare how damp skin feels in still air and in a breeze.
questions.explanation: Evaporating water cools the wetted bulb. The difference becomes small as the air approaches saturation.

questions.prompt: For two atmospheric layers bounded by the same pressure values, which generally has greater vertical thickness?

choices.text: The layer with higher mean virtual temperature
The layer with lower mean virtual temperature
The layer with lower wind speed, regardless of temperature

questions.hint: Compare the column's density with the vertical distance needed for the same pressure change.
questions.explanation: The hypsometric relationship links pressure-layer thickness to mean virtual temperature. A warmer, less dense column is thicker.

questions.prompt: A Northern Hemisphere geostrophic wind blows due east along straight isobars. Where is the lower pressure?
questions.hint: Balance the pressure-gradient force against the deflection associated with the wind.
questions.explanation: Coriolis acts to the right of the eastward flow, toward the south. The opposing pressure-gradient force points north, so lower pressure is north.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified geometry independently: eastward motion has rightward/southward Coriolis; balance requires northward pressure-gradient force. Straight, geostrophic, Northern Hemisphere assumptions are explicit.

questions.prompt: The environment cools 8 degrees Celsius per kilometer. A lifted parcel cools 10 if unsaturated, but 5 if saturated. What stability does this imply?
questions.hint: Compare the parcel with its environment after the same upward displacement.
questions.explanation: An unsaturated parcel becomes colder than its surroundings, while a saturated one becomes warmer. Instability therefore depends on saturation.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified given-rate comparison after 1 km: initially equal-temperature unsaturated parcel ends 2 C colder; saturated parcel 3 C warmer. No external lapse-rate value is needed for the reasoning.
